changes.after: NOAA Forecasts an 83% Chance of a Historic El Niño in October–December
changes.before: NOAA's October El Niño Update Follows a 75% Chance of a Record Event

changes.after: NOAA forecasts an 83% chance of a historic El Niño during October–December 2026, with a three-month relative ocean temperature index of at least +2.5 °C. Strong-to-very strong conditions are likely to continue through January–March 2027.
changes.before: After NOAA's 10 September advisory put 75% odds on a historic El Niño this autumn, the Climate Prediction Center issues its next ENSO discussion on 8 October 2026.

changes.after:
• NOAA’s 8 October 2026 discussion gives an 83% chance of a historic El Niño for October–December, compared with 54% for September–November and 70% for November–January
  • Historic strength means a three-month Relative Oceanic Niño Index (RONI) of +2.5 °C or more, exceeding the strength of previous El Niño events dating back to 1950
  • El Niño strengthened further in September, with the Niño-3.4 index reaching +2.1 °C; strong-to-very strong conditions are likely through January–March 2027
  • The WMO’s September update expects El Niño to persist through February 2027, with risks of floods, drought and extreme heat as rainfall and temperature patterns shift
changes.before:
• The Climate Prediction Center will issue its next ENSO Diagnostic Discussion on 8 October 2026; the 10 September edition kept an El Niño Advisory in force
  • It put a greater than 90% chance on a very strong El Niño during the northern fall and winter of 2026-27
  • For October-December 2026 it gave a 75% chance of a historic event, one stronger than any since 1950 (a three-month RONI of +2.5 °C or more), and reported the Niño-3.4 index at +1.8 °C
  • The WMO separately expects El Niño to persist through at least February 2027, with flooding, drought and heat risks as rainfall patterns shift

changes.after: Nvidia expects roughly 70% revenue growth during fiscal 2028, with chip supply constraining demand. The forecast covers the fiscal year beginning February 1, 2027 and ending January 30, 2028, rather than the August 2026 earnings call on which it was announced.
changes.before: On its August earnings call Nvidia gave its first-ever year-ahead forecast: about 70% revenue growth in the fiscal year ending January 2028, roughly $673 billion, limited by supply rather than demand.

changes.after:
• The estimated growth window is fiscal 2028, February 1, 2027–January 30, 2028, derived from Nvidia’s last-Sunday-in-January calendar policy
  • On its Q2 fiscal 2027 earnings call on 26 August 2026, Nvidia gave its first-ever year-ahead forecast: CFO Colette Kress said fiscal 2028 (ending January 2028) revenue growth would be about 70%, against a 44% analyst average
  • On consensus fiscal 2027 revenue of $396 billion that implies about $673 billion (Fortune puts it at $690-700 billion against analyst projections of roughly $570 billion)
  • Huang said demand is 'much greater than 70%' but supply 'allows us to confidently deliver 70%'; Kress said supply will remain a bottleneck to at least the end of that year, and memory pricing pressures margins
  • Q2 revenue (quarter ended 26 July) was $96.2 billion, up 106% year on year, net income rose 126% to about $60 billion, and Q3 guidance is $108 billion
  • Non-hyperscalers are about half of the business and growing 100% a year; Huang coined 'ACIE' for regional AI companies, neoclouds, startups and enterprises
  • Kress defended against 'circular financing' criticism, citing maximum gross guarantee exposure of $108.5 billion and nearly $50 billion invested in frontier labs
  • Kress expects Vera Rubin to be the fastest product ramp in Nvidia's history, with a $40 billion opportunity for Vera GPUs and CPUs; shares rose over 4% after hours (Fortune)

changes.after: WMO expects the established El Niño to strengthen in the coming months and persist through February 2027, with increased risks of floods, drought and extreme heat. Its September–November outlook already anticipates rainfall and temperature patterns associated with strong El Niño.

  • The WMO says there is nearly a 100% probability that El Niño persists through February 2027; it separately expects further strengthening to very strong intensity
  • Niño 3.4 sea surface temperatures ran +2.2 to +2.6 °C above average from late July to mid-August, with subsurface waters in places more than 8 °C above normal
  • It expects widespread above-normal temperatures over most land areas for September-November 2026 and shifted rainfall, with flooding, drought and extreme heat risks

  • In July the WMO had forecast rapid intensification, noting record heatwaves such as Germany's 41.7 °C in late June and likely drought in Indonesia and Southeast Asia

• Demel was founded in 1786 by Ludwig Dehne, a confectioner from Württemberg, at Michaelerplatz, and moved to Kohlmarkt 14 beside the Hofburg in 1888 after the Burgtheater site was demolished.
  • Emperor Franz Joseph I granted the firm the title K.u.K. Hofzuckerbäcker, confectioner to the imperial and royal court, in 1874.
  • Anna Demel, the first woman made a Councillor of Commerce, kept the house running after the empire fell, and the Anna Torte carries her name.
  • The Dehne and Demel families held it until 1972, when Udo Proksch bought it; after his 1989 arrest in the Lucona affair Raiffeisen Bank took it, and Do & Co acquired it in 2002.
  • From 1954 to 1961 Demel fought Hotel Sacher in court over the 'Original Sacher Torte'; the 1963 settlement gave Sacher the trademark and let Demel sell its own Eduard-Sacher-Torte under a triangular seal.
  • Beside the cafe it runs a museum on its chocolate-making history.

• Confeitaria Colombo was founded in 1894 (an opening in September 1894 is reported) by the Portuguese immigrants Joaquim Borges de Meireles and Manuel José Lebrão, in downtown Rio de Janeiro.

• Henry H. Zietz opened the Buckhorn Exchange on 17 November 1893 as a saloon called the Rio Grande Exchange, in a building put up around 1886 by the Neef Brothers Brewing Company, at 1000 Osage Street in Denver's Lincoln Park.
  • Zietz met Buffalo Bill Cody at age 10 in 1875 and was a scout by 12; Sitting Bull gave him the nickname Shorty Scout for his small frame, and the friendship lasted until Zietz died in July 1949.
  • The saloon served railroaders, cattlemen, miners, gamblers and businessmen, and Theodore Roosevelt dined there in 1905 after his train reached the Rio Grande rail yards, then went big-game hunting with Zietz on Colorado's western slope.
  • When Colorado went dry in 1916, three years before national Prohibition, Zietz turned the front of the saloon into a grocery to stay open; after repeal the business received Colorado Liquor License #1, which is still on display.
  • The walls carry about 500 mounted animals and trophy heads, including a Cape buffalo said to have been shot by Roosevelt, plus a 125-gun collection of Colts and Winchesters from the 1880s and 1890s.
  • Zietz's son Henry Jr. inherited the restaurant; the family sold it in 1978 to Buckhorn Associates, led by Roi Davis and Steve Knowlton, and Bill Dutton is listed as the current owner.
  • The building went on the National Register of Historic Places on 21 April 1983 as the Zeitz Buckhorn Exchange; it bills itself as Denver's oldest continuously operating restaurant, and its best-known dish is Rocky Mountain oysters.

• Caffè Florian opened on 29 December 1720 in the Procuratie Nuove of Piazza San Marco as Alla Venezia Trionfante (Venice the Triumphant), but it was soon known by the name of its first owner, Floriano Francesconi.
  • It is the oldest coffee house in continuous operation in Italy; Antico Caffè Greco in Rome, its nearest Italian rival, dates from 1760.
  • It was the only coffee house that admitted women, which drew Casanova, and its early patrons included the playwright Carlo Goldoni and Goethe; Lord Byron, Marcel Proust and Charles Dickens came later.
  • In the mid-18th century it was one of the few places where Gasparo Gozzi's Gazzetta Veneta could be bought, making it a meeting place for different social classes.
  • The two original rooms grew to four in 1750; in 1796 the State Inquisitors forced Valentino Francesconi to close it because its international clientele had become a gathering point for French Jacobins, and after the French entered Venice in May 1797 he reopened it under the plain name Florian.
  • In 1858 Lodovico Cadorin redecorated it as a set of themed rooms: the Sala del Senato (painted by Giacomo Casa), the Sala Greca, the Sala Cinese and the Sala Orientale; two more rooms followed in 1872 and a Liberty room in 1920.
  • It played a part in the 1848 Venetian Revolution, when the Senate Room was a patriots' meeting point and the café sheltered wounded fighters; from 1893 it hosted exhibitions linked to the Venice art Biennale, and since 1988 its Temporanea installations.
  • Its live orchestra, playing outdoors in the Italian café-concert tradition, is still part of the terrace experience, and a Florence branch on Via del Parione opened in the early 21st century.

• Swan Oyster Depot is at 1517 Polk Street, San Francisco, a marble counter with 18 wooden stools and no tables.
  • It began in the early 1890s as the Cable Oyster Depot of the Lausten family, Danish immigrants who sold shellfish from Fisherman's Wharf.
  • The 1906 earthquake destroyed the original shop; the Laustens rebuilt on Polk Street in 1912 and renamed it Swan, the national bird of Denmark.
  • The Sancimino brothers bought it from the Laustens in 1946; Sal Sancimino widened the menu from shellfish to Pacific fish, and the Combination Salad is a signature.
  • The stools and counter are the same fixtures installed in 1912, and patrons include families across six generations.
  • It won the James Beard America's Classics award in 2000 and is listed by the Michelin Guide.

• Odette opened on 2 November 2015 at 1 St Andrew's Road in National Gallery Singapore, in a 3,100 square foot, 48-seat room.

  • The cooking is modern French with Asian influence and local produce, with signatures such as rosemary-smoked organic eggs, mushroom tea and heirloom beetroot.
  • It won two Michelin stars in 2016 and a third in 2019, when Singapore got two three-star restaurants for the first time.
  • On Asia's 50 Best it entered at No. 9 in 2017 as highest new entry, rose to No. 5 in 2018 and reached No. 1 in 2020.
  • On the World's 50 Best it climbed from 86th in 2017 to 28th in 2018 and 18th in 2019, and by 2025 it was Singapore's sole entry, in its seventh straight year on the list.

• Savoy opened on 3 June 1937 on Eteläesplanadi in Helsinki, at what is now Eteläesplanadi 14, with an interior by Aino and Alvar Aalto furnished by Artek, the company they had founded two years earlier.
  • The Aaltos were commissioned by Harry Gullichsen, chief executive of Ahlström, and his wife Maire Gullichsen, who had co-founded Artek with them.
  • The main dining hall is long and narrow, said to resemble a tram or a ship's saloon, in plywood, wood and brick, with windows over Esplanadi park; in 1937 it had four lifts and air conditioning, advanced for the time.
  • The freeform glass vase Alvar Aalto designed for the interior is still made by Iittala as the Savoy vase, alongside original Artek furniture and lighting.
  • Field Marshal Mannerheim became its best-known regular, visiting two days after opening, and the vorschmack, a dish said to come from an officers' club in Warsaw, and pan-fried pike perch are still on the menu at his table.
  • Roger Moore once visited incognito, until the pianist spotted him and played the James Bond theme.
  • It was named Restaurant of the Year by the Finnish Gastronomic Society in 1999 and 2007; a restoration-minded redesign by Ilse Crawford's Studioilse, with Artek, the Helsinki City Museum and the Alvar Aalto Foundation, came in the early 2020s, and Helena Puolakka is chef patron.

  • The concept is a tasting menu staged as a route through a building: a lounge under a graffiti mural by Michael Shellis, a black-draped archway into a communal dining room with projection-mapped visuals led by a "Mistress of Ceremonies", an open kitchen where the chef serves some courses himself, and a chandeliered dining room hung with Shellis's punk canvases

• Harry Barberian opened Barberian's Steak House at 7 Elm Street in downtown Toronto in 1959, after working as manager-chef at the Le Baron steakhouse and buying the cottage for $6,000.
  • The building dates to 1860, and Harry wanted to keep its character; the original room was built around an open charcoal grill at the front door, with the grill man cooking in view of every guest.
  • Barberian sold a majority share and retired in 1975; his son Arron brought the family back to a controlling stake in 1993 and still owns the restaurant.
  • Arron built a two-storey underground wine cellar at a cost of $1.5 million, with 6.7-metre racks; Wikipedia counts over 20,000 bottles, while a more recent review puts it near 40,000 bottles and a list of about 4,800 selections.
  • The dining rooms hold a collection of Canadiana including original Group of Seven paintings, and patrons have included every Canadian prime minister since John Diefenbaker; Richard Burton and Elizabeth Taylor were reportedly engaged there in 1964.
  • In 2014 the family added a take-out spin-off, TLP Sandwich Co., a few doors away at 15 Elm Street.

changes.after:
• Cafe Batavia opened in 1993 in a restored colonial building on the northwest corner of Fatahillah Square in Jakarta's Kota Tua after the Australian Graham James bought and restored it.
  • The building dates to the 1830s, though some accounts say construction began in 1805, and it is the second-oldest building on the square after the former Batavia city hall, now the Jakarta History Museum.
  • Before becoming a restaurant it had been a residence, a Dutch administrative office, a warehouse and the Paulo Gallery.
  • James bought the neglected structure in 1990, per the Dutch-Australian Cultural Centre, and chose to celebrate its layered past, blending Dutch, Indonesian and international influences.
  • Inside are teak floors, tall windows, a grand staircase, colonial-era portraits and live jazz; the ground floor has a bar and stage and an upstairs Grand Salon seats 150, with a 1930s theme and period photographs.
  • Newsweek International named its Winston Churchill bar The World's Best Bar in 1996, according to Wikipedia.
  • Its reopening became a symbol of Kota Tua's revival, encouraging other restorations around the square and helping make the district a heritage-tourism destination; Indonesian owners now run it.

changes.after: Navi Pillay Wins the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize
changes.before: Norwegian Nobel Committee Names the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize Winner

changes.after: The Norwegian Nobel Committee names South African jurist Navi Pillay as the 2026 peace laureate, recognising her work for peace and international law.
changes.before: The Norwegian Nobel Committee announces the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize in Oslo on 9 October at 11:00 CEST, choosing from 287 nominees (208 individuals, 79 organizations). On 20 September 2026 Kalshi had no clear favourite: Doctors Without Borders at 13%, Sudan's Emergency Response Rooms at 12% and Save the Children at 11%.

changes.after:
• Navanethem “Navi” Pillay won the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize on 9 October. The committee recognised her work advancing peace through international law, making this an award for a jurist’s career rather than a peace agreement between governments.
  • Her work spans South Africa’s struggle against apartheid, international prosecution of atrocities and United Nations human-rights leadership. The committee highlights her service in the Rwanda tribunal and International Criminal Court, and the legal recognition of rape and sexual violence as international crimes.
  • The award comes as international courts and their judges face political pressure. AP places the decision alongside her recent role leading the UN inquiry into Gaza and the reactions of governments that reject that inquiry’s conclusions.
  • The result replaces the September market preview on this pin. Those earlier probabilities were forecasts, not the committee’s shortlist or evidence of a winner; nomination itself is not an endorsement.
  • The announcement occurred in Oslo at 11:00 CEST (09:00 UTC), the time set by the Nobel Foundation. The prize presentation in December is a separate event from today’s announcement.
changes.before:
• The Norwegian Nobel Committee announces the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize on Friday 9 October 2026 at 11:00 CEST, from the Norwegian Nobel Institute (Store Sal, Henrik Ibsens gate 51) in Oslo
  • It is the only one of the six 2026 Nobel announcements whose time is given without the hedge ‘at the earliest’; the others run 5-12 October. The Nobel Foundation's 2 February 2026 press release gives the same schedule
  • The Kalshi market lists the same moment as ‘Oct 9, 5:00am EDT’, with settlement dated Dec 31, 2026
  • There are 287 candidates: 208 individuals and 79 organizations, per the Committee's press release of 30 Apr 2026
  • Wikipedia states the split slightly differently as ‘208 candidates and 79 organisations have been nominated’, and cites a Reuters item headed ‘Some 287 nominated for 2026 Nobel Peace Prize, Trump likely among them’ — the Committee's own release is the authority on the count
  • Kalshi has no clear favourite: Doctors Without Borders at 13% (up 2), Sudan's Emergency Response Rooms at 12% and Save the Children at 11%, on $1,072,760 of volume, with more markets not shown in the capture
  • Kalshi's own table is internally inconsistent on two of those: Emergency Response Rooms shows a 12% chance against a 11¢ Yes price, and Save the Children an 11% chance against a 12¢ Yes price
  • Two of the three Kalshi front-runners are publicly reported nominees: Sudan's Emergency Response Rooms, nominated by the Peace Research Institute Oslo for its volunteer-led grassroots network providing food, medical care and evacuation during the 2023-2026 Sudanese civil war, and Save the Children, nominated by the same institute jointly with Mykola Kuleba ‘for rescuing Ukrainian children’
  • Nominations are secret, but Norwegian parliamentarians and academics may publicise their own choices; publicly reported names include Donald Trump, Volodymyr Zelenskyy and the people of Ukraine, Francesca Albanese, Greta Thunberg, Maia Sandu, Yulia Navalnaya and Pope Leo XIV, and organizations including UNRWA, Yad Vashem, the World Trade Organisation and the city of Minneapolis
  • The Committee cautions that names in the media ‘may come from people claiming to have nominated, or be speculation’, and that proposals and opinions ‘may not be divulged until 50 years have elapsed’
  • Nominations closed on 31 January; the Committee added further names and set a short-list at its first meeting, held on 26 February 2026
  • The prize is worth 9.0 million SEK and is awarded at the ceremony in Oslo on 10 December 2026; the 2025 laureate was Maria Corina Machado

changes.after: The Swedish Academy honours Canadian poet, essayist and translator Anne Carson for an inventive body of work in dialogue with classical literature.
changes.before: The Swedish Academy announces the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature from the Börssalen in Stockholm's old stock exchange, where its permanent secretary opens the doors to say the name aloud.

changes.after:
• The Swedish Academy awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature to Canadian writer Anne Carson on 8 October. The official citation recognises the new literary forms she developed through an inventive dialogue with classical traditions.
  • Carson works across poetry, essays and translation, bringing ancient texts into contemporary writing. AP describes a body of work that crosses genre boundaries rather than an award for one recently published book.
  • Her best-known works include the verse novel Autobiography of Red and the elegy Nox. The choice brings a poet and classicist to a prize often associated with novelists, and follows Canada’s earlier literature laureate Alice Munro.
  • The decision replaces this pin’s announcement preview. The announcement in Stockholm and the medal, diploma and prize presentation on 10 December are different milestones.
  • The Academy’s own Swedish announcement identifies Carson as the laureate; the Nobel Foundation’s English summary confirms that she receives the entire prize share.
changes.before:
• The 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature is announced on Thursday, 8 October, "13:00 CEST at the earliest", at the Swedish Academy (Svenska Akademien)
  • The venue is the Borssalen, Kallargrand 4, Stockholm
  • It is the fourth of six 2026 announcements, which "will take place on 5-12 October", following chemistry on Wednesday 7 October and ahead of the peace prize on Friday 9 October
  • Literature is announced later in the day than the other Stockholm prizes, at 13:00 rather than 11:30 or 11:45 CEST, and like all but the peace prize its time carries the hedge "at the earliest"
  • All prize announcements "will be broadcast live on the official digital channels of the Nobel Prize", with a YouTube live stream listed for each
  • The Nobel Prize YouTube channel's live stream page for this announcement, "Announcement of the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature", was published 2026-09-14T09:52:33Z and says only "The Nobel Prize in Literature will be announced at the Swedish Academy in Stockholm, Sweden"; it names no laureate and gives no announcement date

  • The announcement follows a year-long process: nominations open in September, close at "midnight on 31 January", are considered February to September by a Nobel committee of 5 to 10 members, and the prize-awarding institutions "take a final vote to select their newest laureates" in October
  • The laureate receives their medal, prize money and diploma on Nobel Day, 10 December, in Stockholm
  • The schedule was set out in a Nobel Foundation press release dated 2 February 2026; the nobelprize.org announcement-dates page carries no publication or last-updated date
  • Neither the Academy's practice of opening the doors of the Borssalen nor its permanent secretary is mentioned by any of the three links

changes.before: An eight-storey, 138,000-square-foot building on the former County Family Court site in downtown San Diego, with 125 affordable apartments, a manager's unit and about 4,400 square feet of commercial space. BRIDGE Housing is developing it with the San Diego Housing Commission; VCC Construction finished the framing in July 2026.

changes.after: 1555 Sixth Avenue, San Diego, CA 92101
changes.before: Cortez Hill, Downtown San Diego, California

changes.after:
• BRIDGE Housing’s current target is completion in May 2027. The timeline uses May 31 as the month’s boundary; an exact completion or move-in day is not announced.
  • The eight-story building replaces the former County Family Court site at 1555 Sixth Avenue. Its 126 homes comprise 62 family and individual apartments, 63 supportive apartments for formerly homeless seniors, and one manager’s unit.
  • One-, two-, and three-bedroom homes are intended for households earning up to 60% of area median income. SDHC says the 125 restricted apartments will remain affordable for 99 years.
  • San Ysidro Health will provide resident services. SDHC awarded 84 rental-assistance vouchers: 63 for formerly homeless seniors and 21 for eligible low-income families.
  • Groundbreaking took place April 29, 2025. That announcement and SDHC’s development listing give an earlier early-2027 target; the developer now specifies May 2027.
  • Planned amenities include courtyards, community rooms, laundry, resident parking, and 4,400 square feet of commercial space. Published sources checked do not give rents or an application-opening date.
changes.before:
• "Construction has reached a major milestone at Kindred Affordable Apartments in downtown San Diego, where VCC Construction has completed framing on the eight-story affordable housing development"; "The topping-out milestone marks the completion of the building's structural frame and moves the project closer to its planned opening in early 2027" - a window, not the pin's 1 February 2027 date
  • The 138,000-square-foot development in Cortez Hill "will transform the former site of the County of San Diego's Family Court into an affordable, intergenerational community for seniors and families with low incomes", in a transit-oriented area with access to public transportation, jobs, schools, parks and other community resources
  • It "will include 126 rental homes, community spaces, resident services offices, outdoor courtyards, parking and approximately 4,400 square feet of commercial space", of which "125 affordable apartments and one unrestricted manager's unit"
  • "The affordable homes will remain restricted for 99 years for households earning no more than 60% of San Diego's Area Median Income, currently $99,240 annually for a family of four"
  • It is developed by BRIDGE Housing in partnership with the San Diego Housing Commission, with VCC Construction as general contractor
  • SDHC awarded 84 housing vouchers - "63 vouchers are designated for seniors who have previously experienced homelessness, while 21 will assist eligible families with low incomes" - and provided "a loan of up to $7.955 million using federal, state and local resources", including HUD's HOME Investment Partnerships Program, California's Local Housing Trust Fund and the City of San Diego's Affordable Housing Fund
  • "The County of San Diego contributed $4 million from its Innovative Housing Trust Fund and provided the development site as part of its initiative to use excess county-owned land for affordable housing", and financing includes "more than $17.7 million in recycled tax-exempt Multifamily Housing Revenue Bonds from the state" under a bond recycling partnership with SDHC, the City and the California Housing Finance Agency
  • San Ysidro Health will provide supportive services "including medical and social services through the San Diego Program of All-Inclusive Care for the Elderly (PACE) for seniors who have experienced homelessness", plus case management and social services for all residents
  • SDHC's Colin Miller: "Kindred Apartments will transform this site into a vibrant community that brings seniors and families together and provides housing stability in a shared place to call home"; Mayor Todd Gloria called it an example of "what can happen when public agencies and nonprofit partners work together to deliver much-needed housing"

changes.after:
• The Shanghai Grand Opera House is scheduled to open October 17, 2026, on the Huangpu River in Pudong’s Expo Culture Park. Its inaugural season extends through February 20, 2027, with 47 productions and 82 performances, plus arts education programming. Pudong announcement
  • The venue combines the 2,000-seat Harmony Hall, 1,200-seat Soar Theatre and 1,000-seat Open Stage. The opening concert brings together conductors Yu Long, Zhang Guoyong and Xu Zhong with the Shanghai Symphony Orchestra and Shanghai Opera House Orchestra. Venues and opening program
  • Snøhetta won the international design competition in 2016. In 2019 it was commissioned alongside ECADI, Theatre Projects and Nagata Acoustics as a consortium to deliver the building, connecting architecture, theatre planning and acoustics. Design team’s account
  • The architect describes a public roofscape intended for round-the-clock, year-round community access. That public space gives the building a civic role beyond paid performances; it does not establish that theatre tickets are free. Public roofscape
  • The first season includes La Fenice’s Tosca, the Mariinsky Theatre’s Aida and Staatsoper Unter den Linden’s Der Rosenkavalier, extending the program beyond the opening concert. International productions
  • An October 9 update from Snøhetta reconfirms October 17 and schedules release of its nine-language press kit for 7:30pm Shanghai time. That is the architect’s press launch time, distinct from a confirmed public admission or performance start time. Latest architect update

  • The building was completed in June 2026 after six years of construction, with a "Chinese fan" design and a 10,000-square-meter public landscape platform
  • It holds three performance spaces - the 2,000-seat Harmony Hall, the 1,200-seat Soar Theatre and the 1,000-seat Open Stage, 4,200 seats in all - plus the Grand Atelier arts education space
  • The opening concert, "Shanghai Grand Opera House and Friends", brings together conductors Yu Long, Zhang Guoyong and Xu Zhong with the Shanghai Symphony Orchestra and the Shanghai Opera House Orchestra
  • Three international opera houses appear in the season - Teatro La Fenice with a new "Tosca", the Mariinsky Theatre with "Aida" and Staatsoper Unter den Linden with "Der Rosenkavalier" - which the announcement calls "the first opening season in China" to do so
  • The house states a vision of "becoming an opera palace for the world, a stage for Chinese originals, and a cultural living room for the people"

• On 29 September 2026 the NRC issued TVA a construction permit for a BWRX-300 small modular reactor at the Clinch River Nuclear Site in Oak Ridge, Tennessee, the first such permit for the design in the United States and, in the Breakthrough Institute's words, "the first construction authorization for a commercial small modular reactor in the United States"
  • The NRC completed its review in 14 months, four months ahead of schedule, helped by the Early Site Permit TVA already held for Clinch River, which sets a combined limit of 800 MWe; it is the NRC's second major new-reactor construction approval of 2026 after TerraPower's Natrium in March
  • TVA submitted its construction permit application in April 2025; the BWRX-300 is a 300 MW boiling-water SMR from GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy, and the site sits within the Oak Ridge nuclear ecosystem near the Department of Energy's Oak Ridge National Laboratory
  • The permit allows TVA to build but not to run the reactor: TVA must complete construction and win a separate NRC operating licence before it can load fuel
  • No construction start date has been announced; TVA says it "continues negotiations with industry partners to ensure responsible cost sharing", plans as many as four 300 MW units at the site, and had projected the first BWRX-300 in revenue service by 2032 without committing to a firm date
  • Bechtel was selected to lead construction and Sargent & Lundy the detailed design; the NRC staff's safety evaluation recommended the permit in the summer of 2026

changes.after:
Operator and regulator research, October 11, 2026

The NRC’s Federal Register notice confirms construction permit CPAR-2 for TVA’s Clinch River Nuclear Unit 1 was issued September 28, 2026. It authorizes construction of the reactor facility in Roane County, Tennessee. A construction permit does not establish an operating licence or prove construction has started.

NRC application page provides project and review context; its earlier fall-2026 target is superseded by the issued permit notice.

Earlier pin evidence / inventory snapshot

  • On 29 September 2026 the NRC issued TVA a construction permit for a BWRX-300 small modular reactor at the Clinch River Nuclear Site in Oak Ridge, Tennessee, the first such permit for the design in the United States and, in the Breakthrough Institute's words, "the first construction authorization for a commercial small modular reactor in the United States"
  • The NRC completed its review in 14 months, four months ahead of schedule, helped by the Early Site Permit TVA already held for Clinch River, which sets a combined limit of 800 MWe; it is the NRC's second major new-reactor construction approval of 2026 after TerraPower's Natrium in March
  • TVA submitted its construction permit application in April 2025; the BWRX-300 is a 300 MW boiling-water SMR from GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy, and the site sits within the Oak Ridge nuclear ecosystem near the Department of Energy's Oak Ridge National Laboratory
  • The permit allows TVA to build but not to run the reactor: TVA must complete construction and win a separate NRC operating licence before it can load fuel
  • No construction start date has been announced; TVA says it "continues negotiations with industry partners to ensure responsible cost sharing", plans as many as four 300 MW units at the site, and had projected the first BWRX-300 in revenue service by 2032 without committing to a firm date
  • Bechtel was selected to lead construction and Sargent & Lundy the detailed design; the NRC staff's safety evaluation recommended the permit in the summer of 2026

  • Restart still needed approval from the Nuclear Regulatory Commission plus state and local permits, and investment in the turbine, generator, main transformer and cooling and control systems

Earlier pin evidence / inventory snapshot

  • TerraPower announced on 23 April 2026 the official start of construction of Kemmerer Unit 1, expected to be the first utility-scale advanced nuclear power plant in the United States, following the NRC construction permit
  • NRC commissioners voted on 4 March 2026 to grant the permit, the first for a commercial-scale advanced reactor; TerraPower says the review took 18 months, from an application it submitted in March 2024
  • The 345 MW sodium-cooled fast reactor is paired with a molten-salt storage system that can lift output to 500 MW for more than five hours, and the plant is developed through the Department of Energy's Advanced Reactor Demonstration Program
  • The milestone moves the estimated $4 billion project from early-site and non-nuclear work, which began with a June 2024 groundbreaking, into full plant construction, with about 1,600 workers being mobilised and about 250 full-time staff once operating
  • TerraPower expects the project to be completed in 2030; the site is near a retiring coal facility in Kemmerer, Wyoming

The NRC’s Federal Register notice confirms construction permit CPAR-2 for TVA’s Clinch River Nuclear Unit 1 was issued September 28, 2026. It authorizes construction of the reactor facility in Roane County, Tennessee. A construction permit does not establish an operating licence or prove construction has started.

NRC application page provides project and review context; its earlier fall-2026 target is superseded by the issued permit notice.

Earlier pin evidence / inventory snapshot

  • On 29 September 2026 the NRC issued TVA a construction permit for a BWRX-300 small modular reactor at the Clinch River Nuclear Site in Oak Ridge, Tennessee, the first such permit for the design in the United States and, in the Breakthrough Institute's words, "the first construction authorization for a commercial small modular reactor in the United States"
  • The NRC completed its review in 14 months, four months ahead of schedule, helped by the Early Site Permit TVA already held for Clinch River, which sets a combined limit of 800 MWe; it is the NRC's second major new-reactor construction approval of 2026 after TerraPower's Natrium in March
  • TVA submitted its construction permit application in April 2025; the BWRX-300 is a 300 MW boiling-water SMR from GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy, and the site sits within the Oak Ridge nuclear ecosystem near the Department of Energy's Oak Ridge National Laboratory
  • The permit allows TVA to build but not to run the reactor: TVA must complete construction and win a separate NRC operating licence before it can load fuel
  • No construction start date has been announced; TVA says it "continues negotiations with industry partners to ensure responsible cost sharing", plans as many as four 300 MW units at the site, and had projected the first BWRX-300 in revenue service by 2032 without committing to a firm date
  • Bechtel was selected to lead construction and Sargent & Lundy the detailed design; the NRC staff's safety evaluation recommended the permit in the summer of 2026

Earlier pin evidence / inventory snapshot

  • TerraPower announced on 23 April 2026 the official start of construction of Kemmerer Unit 1, expected to be the first utility-scale advanced nuclear power plant in the United States, following the NRC construction permit
  • NRC commissioners voted on 4 March 2026 to grant the permit, the first for a commercial-scale advanced reactor; TerraPower says the review took 18 months, from an application it submitted in March 2024
  • The 345 MW sodium-cooled fast reactor is paired with a molten-salt storage system that can lift output to 500 MW for more than five hours, and the plant is developed through the Department of Energy's Advanced Reactor Demonstration Program
  • The milestone moves the estimated $4 billion project from early-site and non-nuclear work, which began with a June 2024 groundbreaking, into full plant construction, with about 1,600 workers being mobilised and about 250 full-time staff once operating
  • TerraPower expects the project to be completed in 2030; the site is near a retiring coal facility in Kemmerer, Wyoming

• Hinkley Point C in Somerset is two EPR reactors (2 x 1,630 MWe, 3,260 MWe), owned 76.69% by EDF Energy and 23.31% by China General Nuclear, operated by NNB Generation Company
  • Construction began in March 2017 with completion then expected in 2025; delays are attributed to COVID-19, Brexit and budget overruns

  • Cost is £35bn in 2015 prices, about £48bn at today's prices (up £1.4bn), almost double the initial £18bn estimate
  • Progress per EDF results: Unit 1 civil works 94% by concrete volume, 24 primary loop welds finished in January, safety injection pumps installed; Unit 2 dome lifted and reactor pressure vessel delivered; the M&E programme is still behind
  • Hinkley received £1.6bn from Sizewell C for expertise

  • Timeline: Miliband said mid-2034 for operation and the company's lawyer said both reactors operational by mid-2034; EDF said in 2023 the earliest one reactor could run is end of 2033, so the pin's 2035 estimate is later than these
  • Construction formally began 15 January 2024; in January 2025 the project reported being on time and on budget with GBP 1 billion of savings from replicating Hinkley Point C
  • Opposition includes Together Against Sizewell C and the RSPB over wildlife impact near Minsmere

  • Final investment decision was signed 22 July 2025; stakes are UK Government 44.9%, La Caisse 20%, Centrica 15%, EDF 12.5% and Amber Infrastructure 7.6%
  • Cost is expected at GBP 38 billion as of July 2025, with the National Wealth Fund providing the majority of debt; nearly double EDF's earlier forecast of about GBP 20 billion; bills rise by an average GBP 1 a month during construction
  • Timeline: Miliband said mid-2034 for operation and the company's lawyer said both reactors operational by mid-2034; EDF said in 2023 the earliest one reactor could run is end of 2033, so the pin's 2035 estimate is later than these
  • Construction formally began 15 January 2024; in January 2025 the project reported being on time and on budget with GBP 1 billion of savings from replicating Hinkley Point C
  • Opposition includes Together Against Sizewell C and the RSPB over wildlife impact near Minsmere

changes.after:
• On 8 May 2025 Ontario gave OPG the green light to build the first of four BWRX-300 units at the Darlington New Nuclear Project, the first new nuclear build in the province in more than three decades and the first grid-scale SMR under construction in any G7 country, a month after the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission issued the licence to construct
  • The first 300 MW unit is due in service by the end of 2030 (OPG had earlier anticipated the end of 2029), with the full fleet of four units producing 1,200 MW and the other three planned for the mid-2030s
  • Ontario's energy minister put the first unit at C$7.7 billion, C$6.1 billion for the reactor and C$1.6 billion for systems and services common to all four units; the four-unit plant is estimated at C$20.9 billion
  • By spring 2026 the reactor's steel-and-concrete basemat module had been lifted into the excavated, 35-metre-deep reactor shaft, shortly before 8 May 2026, a year to the day after the final investment decision
  • OPG submitted its licence to operate application for the first unit in March 2026 and it is under CNSC review
  • OPG is drawing on more than 7,000 lessons learned from the Darlington refurbishment, and a tunnel boring machine for the 3.4 km condenser cooling water tunnel was due on site for assembly in early 2026

Date and location

EIA reports operation at month/year precision. The date is the last day of the earliest reported operation month/year, an estimated display boundary, not an exact opening day. Different units may have later dates. Future dates are operator-reported plans, not guarantees.

Coordinates are the EIA-reported plant point, not a verified entrance. New units at existing plants are included; the total excludes older units and battery/pumped storage. Capacity is a power rating, not annual energy output. Status was reported in August and may have changed since.

changes.after:
Operator and regulator research, October 11, 2026

Fermi’s current Project Matador homepage advertises a planned 17 GW private-power/AI campus, about 6 GW permitted and about 2 GW of secured generation assets, with first power targeted for 2026. These are operator development claims, not confirmation that the full campus is operating. The 17 GW headline includes several technologies and must not be recorded as gas generation or added to the separate nuclear pin. EIA’s 11,679.3 MW gas-unit nameplate total and GEM’s initial 6,000 MW gas blocks are different source scopes.

The March 13, 2026 release proposes a further 5 GW gas air-permit application: approximately 11 GW gas plus 4.4 GW nuclear, solar and battery components in a roughly 17 GW campus. Permission and proposed expansion do not demonstrate installed output.

The operator progress page lists an earlier approximately 6 GW gas scope and long-lead equipment. It distinguishes a 478 MW ISO-rated SGT800 package from over 400 MW at site elevation; equipment secured/shipped is not commercial operation.

Date and location

EIA reports operation at month/year precision. The date is the last day of the earliest reported operation month/year, an estimated display boundary, not an exact opening day. Different units may have later dates. Future dates are operator-reported plans, not guarantees.

Coordinates are the EIA-reported plant point, not a verified entrance. New units at existing plants are included; the total excludes older units and battery/pumped storage. Capacity is a power rating, not annual energy output. Status was reported in August and may have changed since.

changes.after:
Operator and regulator research, October 11, 2026

NRC’s Project Matador application page identifies four proposed AP1000 reactors at the Texas campus. Parts 1 and 2 have been accepted for docketing and are under review; Part 3 is targeted for December 31, 2026. The Commission’s combined-licence decision remains to be determined. Application review and an applicant-prepared environmental impact statement do not establish a construction/operating licence or delivered nuclear generation. EIA reports 4,468 MW nameplate across four proposed units.

NRC’s March 23, 2026 release describes public input and the applicant-prepared environmental-review pilot, not licence issuance.

The campus’s advertised 17 GW is a combined development scope, not a nuclear-only rating. First-power marketing for 2026 must not be interpreted as a nuclear commissioning date.

The October 9, 2026 Federal Register notice opens public comment on the draft EIS through November 23. Staff preliminarily recommends licence issuance contingent on successful safety review; a preliminary environmental recommendation is not an issued combined licence.

Operator and regulator research, October 11, 2026

Fermi’s current Project Matador homepage advertises a planned 17 GW private-power/AI campus, about 6 GW permitted and about 2 GW of secured generation assets, with first power targeted for 2026. These are operator development claims, not confirmation that the full campus is operating. The 17 GW headline includes several technologies and must not be recorded as gas generation or added to the separate nuclear pin. EIA’s 11,679.3 MW gas-unit nameplate total and GEM’s initial 6,000 MW gas blocks are different source scopes.

The March 13, 2026 release proposes a further 5 GW gas air-permit application: approximately 11 GW gas plus 4.4 GW nuclear, solar and battery components in a roughly 17 GW campus. Permission and proposed expansion do not demonstrate installed output.

The operator progress page lists an earlier approximately 6 GW gas scope and long-lead equipment. It distinguishes a 478 MW ISO-rated SGT800 package from over 400 MW at site elevation; equipment secured/shipped is not commercial operation.

Operator and regulator research, October 11, 2026

Fermi’s current Project Matador homepage advertises a planned 17 GW private-power/AI campus, about 6 GW permitted and about 2 GW of secured generation assets, with first power targeted for 2026. These are operator development claims, not confirmation that the full campus is operating. The 17 GW headline includes several technologies and must not be recorded as gas generation or added to the separate nuclear pin. EIA’s 11,679.3 MW gas-unit nameplate total and GEM’s initial 6,000 MW gas blocks are different source scopes.

The March 13, 2026 release proposes a further 5 GW gas air-permit application: approximately 11 GW gas plus 4.4 GW nuclear, solar and battery components in a roughly 17 GW campus. Permission and proposed expansion do not demonstrate installed output.

The operator progress page lists an earlier approximately 6 GW gas scope and long-lead equipment. It distinguishes a 478 MW ISO-rated SGT800 package from over 400 MW at site elevation; equipment secured/shipped is not commercial operation.

changes.after:
• The Gambia elects its National Assembly on 10 April 2027, the second of four polls in the Independent Electoral Commission's 2026-2027 calendar: presidential on 5 December 2026, assembly on 10 April, councillors on 22 May, and mayors and chairpersons on 26 June 2027.
  • IEC chairman Joseph Colley announced the calendar at its launch in Bijilo in October 2025, citing Section 43 of the Constitution, which charges the commission with conducting elections and setting their dates. A supplementary voter registration exercise (planned 1 April to 14 May 2026) topped up the 2021 register.
  • The chamber has 58 members: 53 elected from single-member constituencies by first-past-the-post, with the other five appointed by the President. A party therefore needs 29 seats for an outright majority.
  • The baseline is the vote of 9 April 2022, the country's first hung parliament: President Barrow's NPP won 18 seats, the UDP 15, NRP 4, PDOIS 2, APRC 2 and independents an unprecedented 12.
  • The NPP took only about 29% of the assembly vote, against 53% for Barrow in the December 2021 presidential race, and turnout fell to roughly 51% from 89%. The NPP reached 29 seats only by adding its five appointees and allies including the NRP and APRC.
  • That makes 2027 a test of whether the 2026 presidential result carries down to the constituencies, and how many independents hold their seats.

  • The remaining five members, including the Speaker and their deputies, are appointed by the President
  • The Independent Electoral Commission announced the 2026-2027 election dates

changes.after:
• Spain's municipal elections fall on 23 May 2027, the fourth Sunday of May, four years after 28 May 2023. All councillors in about 8,100 municipalities are chosen, including the assemblies of Ceuta and Melilla, along with provincial and island council seats.
  • Councillors are elected by closed-list proportional representation using the D'Hondt method with a 5% threshold per constituency; very small municipalities (under 250 inhabitants) use an open-list system. Mayors are chosen by the new council, and the top list's head takes the post if nobody wins an absolute majority.
  • Regional parliaments are elected the same day in ten autonomous communities (Asturias, Balearic Islands, Canary Islands, Cantabria, Castilla-La Mancha, Valencia, Madrid, Murcia, Navarre and La Rioja), plus the autonomous cities of Ceuta and Melilla. Andalusia, Catalonia, Galicia, the Basque Country and Castilla y Leon vote on their own calendars.
  • In 2023 the PP led with about 31.6% of the vote and 23,442 councillors against the PSOE's 28.1% and 20,790, and the next round is read as a preview of the general election, which must be held by around August 2027.
  • EU citizens resident in Spain may vote only if they register their wish; the statistics institute reported 345,312 already on the roll and mailed 515,363 more, with a 30 December 2026 deadline.
  • Catalonia alone renews 947 town councils with around 9,000 councillor seats, where PSC, Junts, ERC, Comuns and Aliança Catalana are all seeking ground.

changes.after:
• Voters pick a president and vice president on 24 October 2027, and the same day renew 130 of the 257 seats in the Chamber of Deputies and 24 of the 72 Senate seats, drawn from eight provinces (Catamarca, Chubut, Cordoba, Corrientes, La Pampa, Mendoza, Santa Fe and Tucuman). Most governors are also due to be chosen. Voting is compulsory from 18 to 70.
  • A candidate wins in the first round with over 45% of the vote, or 40% plus a lead of more than 10 points. Otherwise the top two meet in a runoff, expected on 21 November 2027. The incoming president takes office when the current term ends on 10 December 2027.
  • Javier Milei, elected in 2023, may seek a second consecutive term and has said he intends to. On the opposition side, Axel Kicillof is among declared candidates, while Cristina Fernandez de Kirchner is barred by a lifetime ban from office.
  • The main live dispute is the PASO, the mandatory simultaneous primaries. They were suspended for the 2025 midterms. The government wants to scrap them or suspend them again for 2027, which needs 37 Senate votes; La Libertad Avanza holds 21 and has said the support is not yet secured.
  • Governors such as Raul Jalil of Catamarca are open to dropping them, calling them an expensive poll, while Tucuman's Osvaldo Jaldo opposes. On 13 August 2026 Kicillof, Sergio Massa and Maximo Kirchner met Peronist governors and agreed to reject elimination or suspension, arguing primaries help order the party's candidacies.
  • Whether the primaries go ahead, due in August under the current calendar, will decide how crowded the first-round field is and how early the government faces a vote on its record.

• Comic-Con 2027 runs Thursday 22 to Sunday 25 July at the San Diego Convention Center, preceded by Preview Night on Wednesday 21 July. Badge sales open first to 2026 attendees on Saturday 17 October 2026, with the general sale for whatever remains on Saturday 14 November.

• Fiscal year 2028 covers 1 October 2027 to 30 September 2028. The Congressional Research Service calls 1 October a hard deadline: the one date in the budget calendar that agencies cannot slip past without either enacted appropriations or a stopgap.
  • Congress is supposed to pass 12 regular appropriations bills. In practice it rarely does: from FY1997 to FY2025 only 25 of 330 regular acts were enacted on or before 1 October, and since FY1998 final enactment has come after the year began, most often in December or March.
  • The usual bridge is a continuing resolution. One has been enacted for every fiscal year since FY1998 and for all but three since FY1977. Full-year CRs funded FY2007, FY2011, FY2013 and FY2025.
  • When no bridge passes, a funding gap forces shutdowns of affected activities. Gaps occurred in FY2014, FY2018 and FY2019 per CRS, and the lapse that began 1 October 2025 lasted 43 days, the longest in US history, ending on 12 November 2025.
  • The path to the date starts with the President's budget, due the first Monday in February, which follows OMB's September agency submissions and fall review; the congressional timetable then targets 15 April for a budget resolution, though most dates are not enforceable.
  • Fiscal 2028 is therefore best read as a deadline rather than a forecast: whether it opens under a stopgap or a full-year deal depends on negotiations that had not started as of October 2026.
changes.before:
• The US federal fiscal year runs 1 October to 30 September, so fiscal year 2028 begins on 1 October 2027
  • Appropriations must be enacted by that date, or the affected agencies lapse into a funding gap
  • The congressional budget timeline works back from this date, with the President's request due the previous February

• The official Atlantic hurricane season runs from 1 June to 30 November. The dates are a convention: they cover the large majority of tropical cyclone formation in the basin, but storms can and do form outside them.
  • The calendar has moved. Weather Bureau seasons once ran June to October; by 1907 the period was 15 June to 15 November, it was extended to 1 June - 30 November in 1917, and settled on those dates by 1965. In 2021, after several years of storms forming before June, the WMO recommended the NHC assess a 15 May start; the NHC now issues routine outlooks from 15 May, but the official season still begins 1 June.
  • The 1991-2020 average is 14 named storms, 7 hurricanes and 3 major hurricanes (Category 3 or higher). The climatological peak is 10 September, with most activity between mid-August and mid-October; the first named storm usually forms in mid to late June and the first hurricane in early to mid-August.
  • Extremes: 2020 had the most named storms (30) and 2005 the most hurricanes (15).
  • The eastern Pacific season starts earlier, on 15 May, and averages 15 named storms, 8 hurricanes and 4 major hurricanes.
  • NOAA publishes its seasonal outlook in late May, before the season starts. The 2025 outlook, released on 22 May 2025, gave 13 to 19 named storms, 6 to 10 hurricanes and 3 to 5 major hurricanes at 70% confidence, with a 60% chance of an above-normal season, and was updated in early August. The 2027 outlook would be expected in the same window.

  • The eastern Pacific season is a fortnight longer at the front, running from 15 May to 30 November. [S]
  • NOAA issues its seasonal outlook for the Atlantic shortly before the season opens — for 2025 it came with a news conference on 22 May. [1]

changes.before: Anthropic's Claude Haiku 5.5, the small, low-cost model of the Claude 5.5 family, is expected in mid-October 2026 after Anthropic said it would follow Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 "in the coming weeks".

changes.after:
• Anthropic released Claude Haiku 5.5 on 7 October 2026, calling it "the cheapest, fastest, and most capable small model we've ever released"; it is the third model of the Claude 5.5 family, after Opus 5.5 (22 September) and Sonnet 5.5 (28 September), both of which had promised it "in the coming weeks"
  • It is available "now on all platforms, including Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure", and on the Claude Platform as claude-haiku-5-5; it is the first Haiku-class model with an adjustable effort setting
  • Anthropic positions it for high-volume, cost-sensitive work such as summaries, compactions, database queries and classification, and as a subagent alongside Opus 5.5 or Sonnet 5.5 on coding; it says Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5 remain better for complex agentic coding

Notable features

  • Price per million tokens for prompts up to 100K tokens is $0.10 input and $0.50 output (cache reads $0.01, cache writes $0.125), against Haiku 4.5's $1 and $5; above 100K tokens it is $0.50 input and $2.50 output. Anthropic puts that at 90% lower than Haiku 4.5 up to 100K tokens, 50% lower above, and about 75% cheaper on average
  • It uses an updated tokenizer, similar to Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5, which takes slightly more tokens per task; Anthropic calls it its fastest model to date at standard speed, though slower than Opus in Fast Mode
  • Safeguards: Anthropic reports major alignment improvements over Haiku 4.5; its cyber safeguards are stricter than Haiku 4.5's and a little looser than other recent models, and still block penetration testing, while its biology safeguards match Sonnet 5, Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5
  • The page does not state a context window; the system card is at anthropic.com/claude-haiku-5-5-system-card

changes.after: Hall and Woodford Win the 2026 Nobel Economics Prize
changes.before: The Royal Swedish Academy Names the 2026 Economic Sciences Laureates

changes.after: Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford share the 2026 economics prize for models built on household and business decisions that help explain how policy can stabilise economies.
changes.before: The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announces the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel, closing the 2026 announcement season. It is the only one of the six not established by Alfred Nobel's will.

changes.after:
• The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences awarded the 2026 economics prize jointly to Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford on October 12 for “microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation”. They share 12 million Swedish kronor equally.
  • Their research rebuilt macroeconomic models around decisions made by individual households and firms. Expectations about future policy help explain spending and pricing, providing a basis for monetary and fiscal measures intended to soften economic fluctuations.
  • Hall is an emeritus economics professor at Stanford and a senior fellow at the Hoover Institution. His university highlights research spanning employment, technology, competition and economic policy.
  • Woodford is Columbia’s John Bates Clark Professor of Political Economy. Columbia describes how the models help central banks and finance ministries choose when to stimulate or restrain activity, and records his comments during the announcement.
  • The official laureate illustrations are by Niklas Elmehed, © Nobel Prize Outreach. They replace the unrelated 2008 news-conference photograph; the existing official announcement video is retained.
changes.before:
• The 2026 Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel is announced on Monday 12 October 2026 by the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, the last of the six 2026 Nobel announcements, which run 5–12 October
  • Both nobelprize.org pages time it as “11:45 CEST at the earliest”, keeping the hedge; only the peace prize announcement is given a time without it
  • The Nobel Foundation press release gives the venue in full as the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, Session Hall, Lilla Frescativagen 4A, Stockholm
  • The YouTube description is vaguer on place, saying only that the prize “will be announced at the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in Stockholm, Sweden”
  • The announcement is broadcast live: “All prize announcements will be broadcast live on the official digital channels of the Nobel Prize”, with a YouTube live stream listed for each
  • The pin's source is that live stream page, titled “Announcement of the 2026 Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel” on the Nobel Prize channel, published 2026-09-14 and tagged #NobelPrize
  • No laureates are named: the live stream page gives no laureate names and no announcement date beyond its own publication timestamp
  • Both pages give the prize its full formal name, “Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel 2026”, setting it apart from the five prizes named for Nobel himself, though neither states that it was not established by his will
  • The press release setting the 2026 dates and venues is dated 2 February 2026, lists a press invitation for this announcement, and says media wishing to attend “should apply to the respective prize-awarding institution in the early fall”
  • The announcement closes a selection year that opens with nominations in September, closes them at midnight on 31 January, runs evaluation from February to September and ends with the institutions' final vote in October
  • The laureates receive their medals, prize money and diplomas on Nobel Day, 10 December, in Stockholm and Oslo
  • On October 7, Polymarket showed approximately $48,536 traded across its economics-prize market. Ariel Pakes was quoted at 19% and Susan Athey at 17%, with individual books below $10,000. These are thin-market trading estimates, not official predictions; inconsistent quotes for other candidates were omitted. Polymarket

changes.before: A batch of 27 satellites for the Starlink mega-constellation - SpaceX's project for space-based Internet communication system. Lifts off from Space Launch Complex 4E, Vandenberg SFB, CA, USA to Low Earth Orbit. The booster is due to land at Of Course I Still Love You.

changes.after:
• Falcon 9 lifted off for Starlink Group 15-25 from Vandenberg at 00:28:11 UTC on October 13, equivalent to 5:28:11 p.m. PDT on October 12. Space Launch Now records “Liftoff.” at that time, replacing the earlier no-earlier-than window.
  • The mission carries a batch of 27 Starlink broadband satellites toward low Earth orbit. The tracker identifies booster B1088 and the droneship Of Course I Still Love You. Satellite deployment and landing outcomes are not inferred from the liftoff update.
  • The operator’s mission page and broadcast are linked by the tracker. The launch window had run from October 12 at 23:00 UTC to October 13 at 03:00 UTC; the pin now records the reported liftoff time rather than the opening of that window.
changes.before:
• Starlink Group 15-25 now targets no earlier than October 12, 2026, with the launch window opening at 23:00 UTC (16:00 PDT). The earlier October 10 and 11 targets have slipped; this remains a planned launch, not a completed flight.
  • The published window runs until 03:00 UTC on October 13. Space Launch Now records the October 8 schedule update and links the mission’s SpaceX page.
  • Falcon 9 is scheduled to carry 27 Starlink V2 Mini optimized broadband satellites into low Earth orbit from Space Launch Complex 4E at Vandenberg Space Force Base, California.
  • The current schedule names booster B1088 for its twentieth flight, replacing the older B1082 assignment. Its first stage is planned to land on the droneship Of Course I Still Love You in the Pacific Ocean.
  • The tracker identifies the mission as a communications launch for the Starlink constellation. Its launch time and flight hardware remain subject to operational changes; verify the mission’s operator page before planning a viewing trip.

changes.after:
• JAXA schedules MMX’s launch on H3 Flight 10 for October 20, 2026 at 04:41:03 Japan Standard Time, equivalent to October 19 at 19:41:03 UTC. The primary announcement confirms the tracker’s UTC instant; the one-day difference is a time-zone conversion.
  • The launch is from the large rocket launch complex at Tanegashima Space Center. JAXA sets a reserve launch period of October 21 through November 7, with a separate launch time to be set for each reserve day.
  • MMX is a planetary-science mission intended to collect samples from Phobos and return them to Earth. The tracker describes a French/German rover accompanying the Japanese probe. These are mission plans, not completed landings or a sample return.
changes.before:
• The launch is recorded as "H3-24 | Martian Moon eXplorer (MMX)", status "Go for Launch" - "Current T-0 confirmed by official or reliable sources" - with NET 2026-10-19T19:41:03Z to second precision and an instantaneous window, window start and end identical
  • An update of 2026-08-19 says "NET October 20" while the T-0 is 19 October: the same instant, since 19:41 UTC on 19 October is 04:41 on 20 October in the pad's Asia/Tokyo timezone. The following day, 2026-08-20, Cosmic_Penguin logged "GO for launch" from a jaxa.jp press release
  • Mission "Martian Moon eXplorer (MMX)", type "Planetary Science", orbit "Mars Orbit": "MMX is a Japanese scientific mission to land on Phobos, one of the two moons of Mars, to collect samples before bringing them back to Earth. The mission includes a small French/German rover to explore the surface of Phobos"
  • The launch service provider is Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, a commercial Japanese agency founded in 1884 with 58 launches, 56 successful, 2 failed, 13 pending and 2 consecutive successes
  • The rocket is the H3 in its "24" configuration - two LE-9 main-stage engines and four SRB-3 solid boosters - expendable, 2 stages, 63.0 m long, 5.27 m in diameter, 7900.0 kg to GTO, takeoff thrust 12142.0 and a launch cost of 50000000; this configuration first flew on 2025-10-26 and has 1 launch, 1 successful, against the H3 family's 9 launches, 7 successful, 2 failed and 8 pending since its 2023-03-07 debut
  • The flight timeline runs booster separations at T+1m56s and 1m58s, fairing separation 3m17s, MECO 4m52s, stage 2 separation 4m59s, first ignition 5m12s, first cutoff 10m40s, second ignition 1h03m57s, second cutoff 1h10m21s and payload separation at 1h11m12s
  • It flies from Yoshinobu Launch Complex LP-2 at Tanegashima Space Center, "the largest rocket-launch complex in Japan ... located on the southeastern tip of Tanegashima, an island located south of Kyushu", established in 1969 with NASDA and now run by JAXA; the pad has 18 launches to date and the site 99
  • The mission had slipped once before: an update of 2023-12-06 recorded it "Delayed to 2026 launch window due to H3 launch vehicle unavailability", followed by "NET October" on 2026-01-07
  • Counting: orbital launch attempt 7413 overall and 240 of the year; the record was last updated 2026-08-20T21:04:48Z, with no webcast, video or info URLs and no mission patches

changes.before: The Bureau of Labor Statistics releases September’s Consumer Price Index at 8:30 a.m. ET on October 14, the inflation print the Fed sees before its October 28 decision. On 20 September 2026 Kalshi put headline CPI above 3.4% at 93% and above 3.6% at 46%, so the market was centred on a 3.5–3.6% year-over-year rate.

changes.after:
• The BLS release calendar schedules the Consumer Price Index for the September 2026 reference month on Oct. 14, 2026 at 08:30 AM, as it does every CPI release
  • Kalshi's KXCPIYOY-26SEP event settles on that release, each strike resolving on whether the Consumer Price Index rose by more than the strike "in the twelve months ending September 2026, as represented by the one-decimal place value reported by the Bureau of Labor Statistics"
  • The rules carry a shutdown clause: "In the case of a delay in data caused by a federal government shutdown impacting the reliability of the Source Agency, the market's latest Expiration Date will be extended to the sooner of the release of the Underlying or six months after the end of the government shutdown"
  • The BLS calendar itself carries no publication or last-updated date, and notes it "is updated as needed with additional news releases, usually at least a week before their scheduled publication date"

  • The market closes Oct 14, 2026 at 8:29am EDT, a minute before the release, with projected payout at 10:05am EDT; its header instead counts down to "Oct 14, 8:00am EDT"

  • The Fed had already moved: Bloomberg reported on Sep 19 that "The Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time since July 2023 and penciled in an additional hike before the end of the year"
  • The equivalent market for November 2026 CPI, settling on the Dec. 10, 2026 release, is priced higher still - Above 3.6% at 59%, Above 3.7% at 50% and Above 3.8% at 40% - so traders expect year-over-year inflation to keep climbing after September

changes.before: The 2028 Summer Paralympics, also known as the Los Angeles 2028 Summer Paralympic Games, and branded as LA28, will be the 18th edition of the Summer Paralympic Games, an international multi-sport parasports event governed by the International Paralympic Committee. The Games are scheduled to take place from August 15 to August 27, 2028, in Los Angeles, California, United States. The pin sits at Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum.

changes.after: SoFi Stadium, 1001 Stadium Drive, Inglewood, CA 90301, USA
changes.before: Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum

changes.after:
• The Los Angeles Paralympic Games open August 15, 2028 and close August 27. They are the city’s first Paralympics and include paraclimbing’s debut.
  • The opening ceremony takes place at SoFi Stadium, named 2028 Stadium during the Games, in Inglewood. This opening pin is mapped to that venue.
  • The Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum hosts the closing ceremony and athletics, making it a different venue from the opening. The wider Games use multiple sites.
  • The organizer’s venue page invites people to sign up for updates but gives no Paralympic opening-ceremony ticket price or public on-sale date. Those details remain unverified.
changes.before:
• The 2028 Summer Paralympics, branded LA28, will be the 18th edition of the Summer Paralympic Games, governed by the International Paralympic Committee and “scheduled to take place from August 15 to August 27, 2028, in Los Angeles, California, United States”
  • They will be Los Angeles’ first Paralympics, the first Summer Paralympics in the United States since Atlanta 1996 and only the third overall; the previous summer edition was Paris 2024 and the next is Brisbane 2032
  • The opening ceremony is at SoFi Stadium, which is called “2028 Stadium” during the Games, and the closing ceremony on 27 August at the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum, where the pin sits
  • The Coliseum will also host athletics for both the Olympics and Paralympics, and will become “the first stadium to have hosted the Summer Olympics three times” in 2028, having staged the 1932 and 1984 Games; its current capacity is 77,500 after the 2018-2019 renovation cut about 16,000 seats, down from 93,607
  • The venue is a National Historic Landmark on a 29.2 acre site at 3911 South Figueroa Street in Exposition Park, opened 1 May 1923 as a memorial to Los Angeles veterans of World War I, jointly owned by the State of California, Los Angeles County and the City of Los Angeles and operated by the University of Southern California under a 98-year master lease implemented in July 2013
  • Its Olympic cauldron, built for 1932 and reused in 1984, has been lit for the venue’s own milestones since May 1, 2023 on the first of each month, and was lit on the evening of 13 September 2017 “while Los Angeles awaited confirmation as host of the 2028 Summer Olympics”
  • Los Angeles got the Games through the twin award of 2024 and 2028: the process was approved at an Extraordinary IOC Session on 11 July 2017 in Lausanne, the IOC named Los Angeles sole candidate for 2028 on 31 July 2017, and both decisions were ratified at the 131st IOC Session on 13 September 2017; the Paralympics follow automatically under a formal IPC-IOC agreement first established in 2001
  • The programme is a record 560 events in 23 sports, up 11 events and one sport on 2024, keeping the 22 sports contested in Paris and adding sport climbing (paraclimbing) for its Paralympic debut; 4,400 athletes are expected
  • Paraclimbing was chosen as the 23rd sport in June 2024 after a record 33 sports applied – including bids to reinstate CP football and sailing and new bids from arm wrestling, beach paravolley, para dance sport, golf, karate, powerchair football, para surfing and wheelchair handball – with the IPC shortlisting paraclimbing and para surfing for the LA28 organizing committee
  • IPC president Andrew Parsons said LA28 would be the most gender-balanced Paralympics in its history: 12 more women’s events (a record 247) and three more mixed or open events than 2024, four fewer men’s events, and a record 17 sports at full gender parity, six more than 2024
  • Athletics is the largest sport at 164 events, followed by swimming (142), cycling (51) and table tennis (32), with climbing making its debut at 8
  • The venue plan was announced on 3 June 2025 and reuses most of the Olympic venues, but SoFi Stadium will not host swimming as it does for the Olympics because the Los Angeles Chargers and Rams need it for NFL preseason games; Paralympic swimming moves to a temporary stadium on the grounds of the Long Beach Convention and Entertainment Center, a decision some Paralympic athletes called an inequity between the Olympics and Paralympics
  • The organizing committee published a first competition schedule on 19 November 2025, and the IPC approved the final schedule and released the dates on 27 May 2026
  • The published calendar runs 13-27 August 2028, two days before the Games’ stated 15 August start, with the first three days carrying no medal events; the daily medal counts as listed sum to 565 in the table’s own total row while the cumulative row ends at 560, the figure the article and infobox both give
  • The emblems for the 2028 Olympics and Paralympics were unveiled on 1 September 2020, stacking the characters “LA” and “28” with an interchangeable “A”; the variant suite includes designs made with Paralympic athletes Scout Bassett (inspired by the infinity symbol), Ezra Frech, Lex Gillette, Jamal Hill and Oz Sanchez

  • Tesla moved the outdoor event from October 1 to October 15 after reviewing severe-weather forecasts with local meteorologists.
  • Invitations identified Waco, Texas. Reports place the demonstration at SpaceX’s McGregor test facility nearby, but the precise venue remains reported rather than independently confirmed.
  • Tesla’s latest teaser shows a full-width light bar. Cold-gas thrusters remain an anticipated feature; their final specifications and production availability are unconfirmed.

changes.before:
• Tesla posted a "Go for launch" teaser on X and put a countdown on its Roadster page, locking in 1 October 2026 for the reveal of the next-generation Roadster.
  • The event is in Waco, Texas, about 90 minutes north of Tesla's Austin headquarters and close to SpaceX's McGregor rocket test site; Tesla has not named the exact venue.
  • It starts at 8:30 p.m. Eastern (5:30 p.m. Pacific, 00:30 UTC on 2 October).
  • Invitations went only to Roadster reservation holders: RSVP before midnight on 16 September, tickets non-transferable, guests 21 and older.
  • The teaser, seen upside down, shows an angular tail, a large rear wing and four plumes from cold-gas thrusters, the SpaceX package Musk has hinted at for years.
  • The reveal is late: Musk set a 1 April 2026 demo at the November 2025 shareholder meeting, then moved it to late April, "a month or so" and August before landing on October.
  • The car was first shown in November 2017 with production promised for 2020; Tesla now targets production at Gigafactory Texas in 2027 or 2028.

Notable features

  • 0-60 mph in 1.9 seconds and a top speed above 250 mph, as claimed in 2017.
  • 620 miles of range from a 200 kWh battery.
  • Optional SpaceX package (code name A71): cold-gas thrusters fed by a composite overwrapped pressure vessel, which Musk says would take 0-60 mph to about 1.1 seconds at roughly 2.75 g; reportedly not street legal.

changes.after:
• Aramis is a 100 MW solar plus 100 MW / 4-hour battery storage project by Intersect Power on about 410 acres at North Livermore Avenue and Manning Road in Alameda County (Cleanview lists the solar at 100 MW and a CAISO queue entry of 101.3 MW; the county EIR also covers the battery and a gen-tie to PG&E's Cayetano substation).
  • Alameda County regulators approved the 100 MW / 138 MWdc project in March 2021; Friends of Livermore had appealed the zoning-board decision over Measure D and zoning concerns.

changes.after: Tesla Reveals Next-Generation Roadster With Thruster Demonstration
changes.before: Tesla Next-Generation Roadster Reveal and Livestream

changes.after: Tesla demonstrated its next-generation Roadster at SpaceX’s McGregor facility on October 15, showing suction-assisted ramp driving and cold-gas-thruster stunts. Consumer production is targeted for 2028; a current production price and public-road approval for the Rocket feature remain unestablished.
changes.before: Tesla schedules its next-generation Roadster reveal for October 15, 2026, with the livestream starting at 7:55 p.m. Central (5:55 p.m. Pacific). The outdoor Texas event was postponed from October 1 because of severe weather; this is a demonstration, not a customer-delivery launch.

changes.after:
• Tesla held its second-generation Roadster reveal on October 15 at SpaceX’s McGregor, Texas test facility. The prior preview can now be read as a reported demonstration, rather than an upcoming announcement.
  • The demonstration combined a suction system with SpaceX-derived cold-gas thrusters for brief airborne maneuvers. It showed a prototype in controlled conditions; the appearance does not establish consumer deliveries or public-road approval.
  • Tesla showed a two-seat Performance configuration, a Thrust version adding rear thrusters, and a single-seat Rocket configuration with additional perimeter thrusters. A demonstrated 0–60 mph run of roughly 0.8 second is a company claim, not an independent instrumented road-test result.
  • Musk said consumer production would start in 2028. Tesla did not set a new production price, and its Rocket feature carries a warning that it is not approved for public-road use. Historical reservation pricing should not be treated as a current offer.
  • The reveal marks a Tesla/SpaceX engineering collaboration, while commercial usefulness, regulatory approval and delivery timing remain separate questions. The new photos show the actual reveal and ramp demonstration, with Tesla credited as the original image source.
  • The pin retains the previously announced 7:55 p.m. Central stream timestamp (00:55 UTC October 16), and the documented move from October 1 because of severe weather. That timestamp identifies the stream, not a newly measured time for the prototype stunt.
changes.before:
• The rescheduled Roadster reveal is October 15, 2026; livestream coverage begins at 7:55 p.m. Central / 5:55 p.m. Pacific (00:55 UTC October 16).
  • Tesla moved the outdoor event from October 1 to October 15 after reviewing severe-weather forecasts with local meteorologists.
  • Invitations identified Waco, Texas. Reports place the demonstration at SpaceX’s McGregor test facility nearby, but the precise venue remains reported rather than independently confirmed.
  • Tesla’s latest teaser shows a full-width light bar. Cold-gas thrusters remain an anticipated feature; their final specifications and production availability are unconfirmed.
  • The 2017 prototype’s acceleration, range and pricing claims are historical targets. The reveal date does not establish when customer deliveries will begin.

  • A qualifying ceasefire is “any mutually agreed suspension of direct military engagement” announced by both countries or confirmed by a consensus of credible reporting and general across the primary theatre; peace deals, truces and holiday ceasefires can count, but informal understandings, unilateral pauses, deconfliction and sector-limited ceasefires do not, and where governments and field reporting conflict “the reporting will take precedence”
